description:
Hey! I’m SaiNayanika Vakkalanka. I code in Python and I’m really into AI that people can actually understand and trust, especially explainable and human-centered ML. I also like computer vision and AI for education, and I’ve done research work in that area.

For this challenge I want to build astronaut health monitoring software that doesn’t just flag problems but explains why, so the crew and doctors can trust what it’s telling them.
summary:
A message from Mars can take up to 24 minutes to reach Earth, so a crew has to notice a health problem before a doctor can reply. Orbit Check is an app that helps astronauts do that through a daily check-in.
Each day the astronaut logs heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood and radiation dose. The app compares every reading with medical safe ranges and with the astronaut’s own last 14 days. It marks each reading green, amber or red, explains the flag in plain words and gives a next step.
The app has five mission settings: space station, deep-space spacecraft, lunar rover, Moon base and Mars base. Each setting has its own radiation limits, daily routine and priority measurements. A routine on the mission clock prompts each measurement. XP, badges and a daily quiz reward regular logging.
The app uses NASA data. Solar particle events from NASA DONKI (2021 to 2025) are replayed on their real dates as radiation alerts. Inspiration4 crew blood tests from NASA OSDR are charted against the app’s ranges. NASA’s list of ISS research equipment is matched to each measurement.Orbit Check is a prototype with simulated demo readings, not a medical device.
details:
What it does

Orbit Check is a web app that an astronaut opens once a day. They log heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, hours slept, mood and the day’s radiation dose. They can also tick symptoms such as a headache or a change in vision.

The app marks each reading green (“All good”), amber (“Heads up”) or red (“Act now”). Every flag has a short explanation, the NASA spaceflight hazard it relates to and a next step. The app says when to contact the flight surgeon, and it ca n write a plain-text summary of the day to send.

How it works

Each reading gets three checks:

1. Safe range. The ranges come from the American Heart Association, the CDC and the American Diabetes Association, plus bands our team set. All of them are in thresholds.md in the repo.

2. Personal baseline. A reading 3 or more standard deviations from the astronaut’s own last 14 days is flagged, even inside the safe range.

3. Whole-day check. An Isolation Forest model flags a day whose readings, taken together, look unlike the earlier days of the mission.

The app also flags three nights in a row under 6 hours of sleep, three days in a row with mood at 2 or lower, a blood pressure of 180/120 or higher, and any day with a NASA-recorded solar particle event.

The astronaut chooses one of five settings: space station, deep-space spacecraft, lunar rover, Moon base or Mars base. The setting changes the expected daily radiation dose, the radiation limits, the daily routine and the three measurements the app checks most closely. In deep space, on a rover and on Mars, two amber flags in a day are enough for the app to recommend contacting the flight surgeon. On the station and the Moon base it takes three.

The app also has:

- A daily routine on the mission clock (UTC) that shows which measurement or task is due now

- XP, six levels, a streak, 10 badges, a daily quiz and a crew leaderboard, where points come from logging and healthy habits and never from the health numbers

- Trends tab with a color grid of the whole mission, a chart for each measurement and a running radiation total against the 600 mSv career limit

- A sleep tracker that records bedtime and wake time with two taps

-A voice check that suggests a mood score from a 5 to 10 second recording

- A “Did you mean that?” question before it saves a reading that looks like a typing mistake, such as a heart rate of 660

- A separate log for each crew member, saved in a SQLite database, with an optional PIN and a profile photo

NASA data

-NASA DONKI: solar energetic particle events from 2021 to 2025. The demo mission replays them on their real calendar dates, so a storm NASA recorded becomes a radiation alert.

-NASA Open Science Data Repository: blood tests from the four Inspiration4 crew members (studies OSD-575 and OSD-569), charted against Orbit Check’s ranges.

-NASA Space Station Research Explorer: 36 human-research equipment items and about 370 experiments, matched to each measurement. On that list, no ISS research device measures mood, and the devices for blood sugar and sleep are older equipment.

-NASA Human Research Program: the five hazards of human spaceflight and the named health risks shown with each flag.

-Curiosity’s RAD instrument: 1.84 mSv a day in deep space and 0.64 mSv a day on the surface of Mars, used as the expected dose in those settings.

Benefits and intended impact

Most astronauts are not doctors. Orbit Check is meant to help a crew member notice a problem early and know when to ask for help. The daily log also gives the flight surgeon one summary of readings, flags, symptoms and sleep.

Tools

We wrote Orbit Check in Python 3.11. It uses Streamlit for the web app, Plotly for the charts, pandas and NumPy for the data, scikit-learn for the Isolation Forest and for training the voice model, SciPy for the audio measurements, Pillow for photos and SQLite for storage. The repo has 75 automated tests that run with pytest.

We worked in GitHub Code spaces. The app needs no special hardware. The photo and voice features use the browser’s camera and microphone.

What is creative about it

-The demo mission replays NASA’s recorded solar particle events on their real dates, so the radiation alerts match storms that happened.

-Each mission setting has its own three priority measurements, and the app recommends calling the flight surgeon sooner when help is farther away.

-Points reward logging and never the health numbers, so there is no reason to enter a better number than the real one.

-We matched NASA’s list of ISS research equipment to our measurements. The list has no device for mood, so we trained a small voice model that suggests a mood score.

What we considered

-Every flag is explained in everyday words, and the Guide tab has steps for taking each measurement.

-Every color comes with a word, for people who find colors hard to tell apart.

-Voice recordings are analyzed in memory and never saved. A crew member can lock their log with a PIN, and only a salted hash of the PIN is stored.

-The voice model picks the right mood 63% of the time on actors it never heard, and 58% with background noise. Guessing would get 25%. It was trained on recordings of actors (the RAVDESS dataset), so it only suggests a score and the astronaut decides.

-The demo astronaut’s readings are simulated. Orbit Check is a prototype and not a medical device.

Use of AI

We used Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, to help write, debug and test the code, to help analyze the NASA datasets and to help write the documentation. The README also credits Claude. No image, video or audio in the project is AI-generated. The photos come from the NASA Image and Video Library.
